When a model decides how to decompose a problem, it often makes mistakes. In the original RLM setup, these fundamental decisions are completely invisible to the human operator. The chain of failure starts quietly. The model writes a flawed search filter or it selects an arbitrary boundary to chunk a text file. The physical consequence is immediate. A critical semantic unit of data is split directly in half. Now, a recursive submodel is asked to verify an answer based on incomplete text. Because it can only see half the context, it attempts to invent a logical connection that isn't actually there, it hallucinates.

The system stitches these findings together and delivers an answer that is confidently wrong, while the root error remains entirely hidden behind the clean interface of the execution environment. If an autonomous model writes a flawed filter, it permanently blinds itself to the evidence before any actual reasoning even begins. This creates a dangerous new class of failure. Prior academic frameworks recognized this opacity.
